topic: Conditionals and Control Flow in Rust

questions.title: What does the code block `{ let x = 5; x * 2; }` evaluate to?
options: A compiler error due to missing explicit return
questions.explanation: The code block ends with a statement terminated by a semicolon `;` (`x * 2;`), so it evaluates to the unit type `()`.

questions.title: Which of the following conditions in an `if` expression will cause a compile error?
options: if x { ... } (where x is 1 of type i32)
questions.explanation: In Rust, the condition in an `if` statement must evaluate strictly to `bool`. Unlike C/C++, integers (such as 1) are not implicitly cast to booleans.

questions.title: What is the critical requirement for `if-else` branches when used as an expression to assign a value?
options: They must return an integer type
They must be enclosed in parentheses
Both branches (if and else) must evaluate to identical types
The else branch must be omitted
questions.explanation: Because `if-else` is an expression, both branches must produce values of the exact same type so the compiler can infer a single unambiguous type for the variable.

questions.title: What does `let u = if x > 100 { foo() };` evaluate to if foo() returns i32 and x is 50?
options: A compilation error (type mismatch between i32 and ())
questions.explanation: Without an `else` branch, the default value when the condition is false is `()`. Because the `if` branch returns `i32`, the compiler fails due to mismatched branch types (`i32` vs `()`).

questions.title: Which logical operator combines multiple `let` pattern bindings and conditions in an `if let` chain?
questions.explanation: In `if let` chains (let-chains), pattern bindings and boolean predicates are sequenced using the conjunction operator `&&`.
